messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Curriculum Designer
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is a 46-year-old African American man who works as a curriculum designer for a large public-school district. He is married and had been used to thinking of himself as steady, thoughtful, and composed, someone who spent his days shaping lesson plans, revising materials, and moving between meetings with teachers and administrators. The event that now returns to him happened on an ordinary workday evening, after he had left the district office with a laptop bag full of drafts and notes. He had been pulled over by police while driving home. What began as a traffic stop escalated quickly. He remembers the flashing lights filling his rearview mirror and then the officer’s voice, already sharp before Kwame had fully understood why he had been stopped. When he reached, as instructed, toward the center console where his registration was kept, the officer shouted, drew his weapon, and ordered him to freeze. Within moments Kwame was out of the car, pushed against it, and handcuffed. He recalls the pressure of metal against his wrists, the heat of the hood against his cheek, and the terrifying certainty, in those minutes, that a small movement or misunderstood word could get him killed.

What remains most vivid is not a coherent story he can easily tell from beginning to end. Instead, the memory comes back in pieces that feel too large for words. In the first weeks after it happened, when his wife asked him to explain what the stop had been like, he would start and then fall silent. He could describe fragments—the lights, the yelling, the gun—but then his face would tighten and he would stop talking altogether, as if language failed him right where the fear had peaked. He has told his therapist that he cannot seem to put the worst part into words. At times there is not even a picture in his mind, only the same surge of dread flooding his body, as if the emotional force of the event arrives before any image does. A sound behind him, a sudden command barked across a hallway, or the flare of police lights on a nearby street can bring that feeling down on him so strongly that he has to sit still and wait for it to pass.

Over the months that followed, Kwame became markedly watchful. He noticed every patrol car on the road and tracked officers’ movements with exhausting precision whenever he passed them in parking lots, near gas stations, or outside the schools he visited for work. In school buildings he began choosing windows and doorways carefully, scanning the hall before stepping out of conference rooms. If a security officer entered a campus office unexpectedly, Kwame’s body reacted before he had time to think; his shoulders jumped, his chest tightened, and his heart pounded hard enough that he sometimes lost track of what had just been said in a meeting. Colleagues occasionally saw him startle at a slammed door or at the crackle of a radio and would pause, confused, while he tried to recover and continue discussing curriculum maps as though nothing had happened.

His job has made these moments difficult to avoid. Part of his role involves visiting schools across the district, and some campuses have visible police presence or school resource officers near the front entrance. On those mornings, Kwame has found himself sitting in his car for several extra minutes, gripping the steering wheel and steadying his breathing before he can make himself go inside. He does not tell coworkers why. He has come to believe that if he lets the memory open fully, he will be swallowed by it. Even in therapy, when he begins to approach the moment the officer drew the gun, his voice trails off and he asks to stop because the emotion arrives too fast and too intensely.

At home, his wife has noticed how sharply he reacts to sudden noises and how often he positions himself to keep an eye on the street through the front window. He is not describing elaborate theories about danger; it is more immediate than that. He feels on guard, as if his body has decided that being less than fully alert would be reckless. What frightens him most is the force of the reactions themselves—the way he can be pulled into terror by a siren, flashing lights reflecting off another car, or an authoritative voice raised without warning. He sought help after a recent school visit where a police officer turned abruptly toward him in a hallway and greeted him, and Kwame recoiled so visibly that a teacher asked if he was all right. He was ashamed by how exposed he felt, and shaken by how quickly his body had acted as though the stop were happening again. Coming into treatment, he says he wants to be able to speak about what happened without shutting down, and he wants, more than anything, to stop living as if the next ordinary interaction could turn lethal in an instant.
